verifiedClaims.claim: In South Carolina, that crash creates a civil claim against the driver, their insurer, often the bar or restaurant that over-served them, and your own uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage when the at-fault driver flees or can't pay.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 38-77-150, 38-77-160, 38-77-170 (UM/UIM); §§ 61-4-580(A)(2), 61-6-2220 and Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill, 388 S.C. 407 (2010) (server liability)
verifiedClaims.note: Each pathway has a statutory or case-law footing. The UM 'flees' pathway is conditioned by § 38-77-170 (see the hit-and-run claims below).

verifiedClaims.claim: You have three years from the crash date to file under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-3-530
verifiedClaims.note: § 15-3-530(5): three years for 'any injury to the person or rights of another, not arising on contract'. Matches the writer-profile table. Format only: the profile's strict citation form is 'S.C. Code § 15-3-530' without 'Ann.'; the post uses 'S.C. Code Ann.' throughout (editor's call, not a factual error).

verifiedClaims.claim: that clock does not stop because the driver was a Memorial Day visitor from Ohio
verifiedClaims.note: Nuance for the editor, not an error: § 15-3-30 nominally tolls limitations while a defendant is out of state, but the Supreme Court refused to apply it where the plaintiff knew the defendant's whereabouts and substitute service was available (Meyer v. Paschal, affirming that the tolling statute's purpose is 'frustrated' in that situation). A nonresident motorist is always servable through the DMV Director under § 15-9-350, so treating the three years as firm is the correct advice.

verifiedClaims.claim: Deadline: SC personal-injury claims must be filed within 3 years under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-3-530; wrongful-death under § 15-51-10.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Three years for personal injury under S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5); wrongful death also three years, under § 15-3-530(6), running from the date of death. § 15-51-10 creates the wrongful-death cause of action and § 15-51-20 requires the executor or administrator (personal representative) to bring it; neither sets the deadline.
verifiedClaims.note: The three-year period is right; the citation for it is § 15-3-530(6), not § 15-51-10. Suggested: 'wrongful death within 3 years of the death under § 15-3-530(6), brought by the estate's personal representative (§ 15-51-20)'. The same miscite recurs in the body SOL paragraph, the fatal-crashes bullet and faq:0.

verifiedClaims.claim: Fault rule: 51% modified comparative negligence — you recover if you're 50% or less at fault (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243 (1991)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (S.C. Jan. 7, 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Citation confirmed on CourtListener (303 S.C. 243; 399 S.E.2d 783; decided 1991-01-07). Rule: plaintiff recovers 'if his or her negligence is not greater than that of the defendant', reduced proportionally. Correctly attributed to Nelson and not to § 15-38-15 (profile rule). Also verified verbatim in sibling packs 1653/2647/4738.

verifiedClaims.claim: Hit-and-run: Leaving an injury crash is a felony under S.C. Code Ann. § 56-5-1210 — and triggers your own UM coverage even when the driver is never found.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Under S.C. Code § 56-5-1210(A), leaving the scene of an injury crash is a misdemeanor (30 days to 1 year) when injury but not great bodily injury or death results; it is a felony only when great bodily injury (30 days to 10 years) or death (1 to 25 years) results. UM coverage for an unknown driver is available under § 38-77-170 only if the crash was reported to police within a reasonable time AND either there was physical contact with the unknown vehicle, an independent witness signs an affidavit, or the insured has an electronic recording of the crash.
verifiedClaims.note: MOST CONSEQUENTIAL LEGAL ERROR, published five times (this bullet, two body passages, the hit-and-run subsection, faq:1). § 56-5-1210(A)(1): 'a misdemeanor ... when injury results but great bodily injury or death does not result'; (2) and (3) are the felonies. Suggested: 'Leaving an injury crash is a crime under S.C. Code § 56-5-1210 — a felony when it causes great bodily injury or death — and your own UM coverage applies to an unidentified driver if you reported the crash promptly and there was physical contact, an independent witness, or a recording (§ 38-77-170).' Renders above the article.

verifiedClaims.claim: Stacked coverage: SC allows UM (§ 38-77-150) and UIM (§ 38-77-160) stacking across household vehicles — often the only money in a hit-and-run or out-of-state-rental case.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: UM is mandatory on every policy at the § 38-77-140 minimums (§ 38-77-150); UIM must be offered at the insured's option (§ 38-77-160). Stacking is limited, not general: § 38-77-160 provides that an insured with UM/UIM above the basic limits 'is protected only to the extent of the coverage he has on the vehicle involved in the accident', and if none of the insured's vehicles was involved, 'only to the extent of coverage on any one of the vehicles with the excess or underinsured coverage'. Case law confines stacking to Class I insureds (named insured, spouse, resident relatives); Carter v. Standard Fire Ins. Co., 406 S.C. 609, 753 S.E.2d 515 (2013) voided a policy exclusion that conflicted with that statutory right.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire Insurance, 406 S.C. 609 (2013)
verifiedClaims.note: Same finding as sibling packs 1757 and 4738: § 38-77-160 is not a stacking statute; it caps stacking. Suggested: 'SC lets a named insured or resident relative (a Class I insured) stack UM/UIM from other household vehicles and policies, capped at the coverage on the vehicle involved (§ 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire, 2013) — often the only money in a hit-and-run or out-of-state-rental case.' Carter opinion also at https://law.justia.com/cases/south-carolina/supreme-court/2013/27340.html and https://static.case.law/sc/406/cases/0609-01.json. Repeated in the pathways table and faq:1.

verifiedClaims.claim: Felony DUI: Causing great bodily injury or death is felony DUI under S.C. Code Ann. § 56-5-2945; criminal restitution runs parallel to your civil case.
verifiedClaims.note: § 56-5-2945(A): DUI proximately causing great bodily injury or death is 'felony driving under the influence' — mandatory 30 days to 15 years (GBI) or 1 to 25 years (death), no suspension or probation. Restitution is not in § 56-5-2945; it is ordered under the general victim-restitution statute, § 17-25-322(A) ('in addition to any other sentence'). Optional precision: cite § 17-25-322 for the restitution clause.

verifiedClaims.claim: Local venue: Civil suits are filed in the Horry County Court of Common Pleas (15th Judicial Circuit) in Conway; claims of $7,500 or less go to magistrate's court.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Horry County Courthouse, 1301 Second Avenue, Conway, SC 29526; Judicial Circuit 15 (Horry and Georgetown). Magistrates have concurrent civil jurisdiction where damages claimed do not exceed $7,500 (§ 22-3-10(2)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SC Judicial Branch courthouse search (Horry); S.C. Code § 22-3-10
verifiedClaims.note: Both facts verified. Cosmetic: magistrate jurisdiction is concurrent, so 'can go to' is more exact than 'go to'. Same figure verified in sibling pack 4738 (§ 22-3-10, https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t22c003.php).

verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Strand Medical Center is at 5050 Hwy 17 Bypass S, Myrtle Beach, SC 29588 — on US-17 Bypass on the Socastee/Myrtle Beach side, not in the Murrells Inlet area — and is Grand Strand Health's freestanding satellite campus with a 24/7 ER, not a hospital. The nearest hospital ER is Tidelands Waccamaw Community Hospital, 4070 Highway 17, Murrells Inlet, about 5.9 miles south of central Surfside Beach.

verifiedClaims.currentValue: SCDPS Traffic Collision Fact Book 2024 Edition (NHTSA imputed BAC .08+): South Carolina alcohol-impaired-driving fatalities were 319 of 1,066 (30%) in 2020, 406 of 1,198 (34%) in 2021, 471 of 1,094 (43%) in 2022, 428 of 1,047 (41%) in 2023 and 417 of 1,038 (40%) in 2024 (preliminary). The US share was 30–32% in each of those years.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Traffic Collision Fact Book 2024 Edition, p. 72 ('Alcohol Impaired (.08+) Driving Fatalities — GA, NC, SC and the US')

The 23–28% range matches Georgia's column in the same table, which suggests the wrong column was read.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina changed these rules for claims arising after 1 January 2026. The 2025 Act narrowed the alcohol exception in S.C. Code § 15-38-15 and created § 61-2-147, under which an establishment can be jointly and severally liable for fifty percent of a plaintiff’s actual damages where a verdict is returned against both it and a driver charged with DUI
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 2025 Act No. 42 (H.3430), effective January 1, 2026, 'applies only to causes of action or claims arising or accruing after January 1, 2026'. New § 61-2-147(A): 'If a verdict is rendered against both a licensee and a defendant charged under Section 56-5-2930, 56-5-2933, or 56-5-2945, then the licensee is jointly and severally liable for fifty percent of the plaintiff's actual damages.' New § 15-38-15(F) keeps joint and several liability for wilful, wanton, reckless, intentional or illegal-drug conduct but no longer lists 'the use, sale, or possession of alcohol' (the pre-2026 (F) did). § 61-6-2220 now bars sales 'knowingly' made to intoxicated persons.
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate. 'Narrowed' is fair: the alcohol carve-out was removed from § 15-38-15 and replaced by the 50% rule in § 61-2-147. The § 61-2-147 rule turns on the driver being charged under §§ 56-5-2930, -2933 or -2945 — 'charged with DUI' covers it. Internal link target /resources/south-carolina-liquor-liability-2026/ not checked here.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-3-530, you have three years from the crash date to file a personal-injury lawsuit. Wrongful-death claims under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-51-10 follow the same three-year period from the date of death.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Personal injury: § 15-3-530(5), three years. Wrongful death: § 15-3-530(6), three years 'to begin to run upon the death of the person'; the action itself arises under § 15-51-10 and is brought by the personal representative (§ 15-51-20).
verifiedClaims.note: Substance correct; cite the deadline to § 15-3-530(6). Suggested: 'Wrongful-death claims (S.C. Code § 15-51-10) carry the same three years, running from the date of death under § 15-3-530(6).'

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina follows modified comparative negligence with a 51% bar, set in Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243 (1991). You recover if your share of fault is 50% or less, reduced by your percentage; at 51%+ you take nothing.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Correct and correctly attributed to Nelson, not § 15-38-15.

verifiedClaims.claim: SC's DUI statute (§ 56-5-2930) and its DUAC companion (§ 56-5-2933) cover the standard misdemeanor. If the drunk driver caused great bodily injury or death, prosecutors can charge felony DUI under § 56-5-2945 — with mandatory prison time and court-ordered restitution.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified. Mandatory imprisonment under § 56-5-2945(A) is 30 days–15 years (GBI) or 1–25 years (death), no suspension or probation; 'great bodily injury' is defined in (B). Restitution comes from § 17-25-322, which the editor may cite. First and second DUI offenses under §§ 56-5-2930/-2933 are misdemeanors; penalties escalate for third and later offenses.

verifiedClaims.claim: The civil claim is separate, but the criminal record (BAC, breath, dashcam, body cam) becomes some of your strongest evidence.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-2953 (incident-site and breath-test-site video recording mandatory for §§ 56-5-2930, -2933, -2945 arrests)
verifiedClaims.note: Stronger than the post says: § 56-5-2953(A) requires video from no later than blue-light activation through the field sobriety tests and arrest, and at the breath-test site. Optional add: cite § 56-5-2953.

verifiedClaims.claim: SC common-law negligence (no separate dram-shop statute)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina has no dram-shop act, but server liability is not bare common-law negligence: it is negligence per se built on the criminal sale statutes — § 61-4-580(A)(2) (beer/wine permit holders may not 'knowingly ... sell beer or wine to an intoxicated person') and § 61-6-2220 (liquor licensees may not sell 'to persons in an intoxicated condition', 'knowingly' from 2026) — recognized in Tobias v. Sports Club, Inc., 332 S.C. 90, 504 S.E.2d 318 (1998) and Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill, Inc., 388 S.C. 407, 697 S.E.2d 558 (2010). For claims arising after January 1, 2026, § 61-2-147 adds the 50% joint-and-several rule when the driver is charged with DUI.
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested cell: 'Negligence per se under §§ 61-4-580 / 61-6-2220 (no dram-shop act; Tobias, Hartfield); § 61-2-147 for post-2026 claims'. Same correction applies to faq:4. Tobias: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1358670/tobias-v-sports-club-inc/ ; Hartfield: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1347026/hartfield-v-getaway-lounge-grill-inc/

verifiedClaims.claim: Criminal restitution does not reduce your civil judgment
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 17-25-322 orders restitution 'in addition to any other sentence' in the criminal case and says nothing about setoff against a civil judgment; no provision of Title 17, Chapter 25 addresses the interplay either way.
verifiedClaims.note: The categorical 'does not reduce' cannot be sourced to the statute, and general double-recovery principles cut the other way for amounts actually paid for the same loss. Suggested cell: 'Restitution is ordered in the criminal case (§ 17-25-322) and is no substitute for the civil claim'.

verifiedClaims.claim: A drunk driver in a Hertz or Turo rental creates a three-way coverage fight: the rental company's policy, the renter's personal auto policy, and your UM/UIM.
verifiedClaims.note: Characterization; the UM/UIM leg is statutory. Editorial note only: Turo is a peer-to-peer car-sharing platform rather than a rental company, so 'rental company's policy' fits Hertz better than Turo.

verifiedClaims.claim: the rideshare company's $1M third-party policy kicks in when the driver is in Period 2 (en route to pickup) or Period 3 (carrying a passenger)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: S.C. Code § 58-23-1630(C)(1): while a TNC driver is 'engaged in a prearranged ride', primary liability insurance of 'at least one million dollars for death, bodily injury, and property damage'. § 58-23-1610 defines a prearranged ride as 'beginning when a driver accepts a ride requested by a rider ... continuing while the driver transports a requesting rider, and ending when the last requesting rider departs'. Logged on but not matched (§ 58-23-1630(B)): $50,000 / $100,000 / $50,000.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified: 'en route to pickup' falls inside the statutory prearranged ride. Optional: cite § 58-23-1630.

Crash figure available: SCDPS Fact Book 2024, Horry County vulnerable road users — 336 motorcyclists injured or killed in 2024 collisions, 11 of them fatally. No source apportions Horry County catastrophic crashes to the rally weeks.

Horry County crashes injured or killed 336 motorcyclists in 2024, 11 of them fatally (SCDPS Fact Book 2024) — talk to ...'

verifiedClaims.claim: Walkers crossing to the beach and golf carts entering 45 mph traffic from N Lake Drive get hit by DUI drivers more often than official statistics suggest.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: SCDPS Fact Book 2024, Horry County: 110 pedestrians injured or killed in 2024 collisions, 12 of them fatally. Golf carts may legally only cross a road posted above 35 mph at an intersection, not travel on it (§ 56-2-90(D)(4)). 'More often than official statistics suggest' is unfalsifiable and unsourced.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS Fact Book 2024 Horry County page; S.C. Code § 56-2-90
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Walkers crossing to the beach and golf carts crossing 45 mph traffic at N Lake Drive are the most exposed road users on this stretch — Horry County crashes injured or killed 110 pedestrians in 2024, 12 of them fatally (SCDPS Fact Book 2024).' 'Entering' → 'crossing' to match § 56-2-90.

verifiedClaims.note: General characterization (vicarious liability / commercial auto coverage); no figure or statute asserted.

verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'the case is brought by the estate's personal representative (§ 15-51-20), and the three-year clock under § 15-3-530(6) runs from the death.' Matches the writer-profile wrongful-death row.

verifiedClaims.claim: Hit by a drunk driver on South Kings Highway (US-17 Business) through Surfside Beach? A Grand Strand DUI-crash guide to your South Carolina rights, deadlines, and the insurance pathways that actually pay.
verifiedClaims.note: No checkable figure or statute; corridor naming is correct (South Kings Highway carries US-17 Business through Surfside Beach). Publishes as the Article description.

verifiedClaims.claim: In South Carolina, you have three years from the crash date to file a personal-injury lawsuit under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-3-530. Wrongful-death claims under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-51-10 also follow a three-year deadline from the date of death.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Personal injury: three years, § 15-3-530(5). Wrongful death: three years from the date of death, § 15-3-530(6); § 15-51-10 is the cause of action.
verifiedClaims.note: Deadline correct; cite it to § 15-3-530(6). Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Narrow exceptions (minors, incapacitated plaintiffs, government defendants) can shift the timing.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Minors and persons insane at accrual: tolling under § 15-3-40. Government defendants: the Tort Claims Act SHORTENS the period to two years from discovery (§ 15-78-110), extended to three years only if a verified claim was first filed.
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate as a hedge. Worth a clause that the government exception runs the other way: 'two years under § 15-78-110 if a government vehicle or agency is a defendant' (writer-profile table row).

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Leaving an injury crash is a felony under S.C. Code Ann. § 56-5-1210, and the hit-and-run police report is what triggers your own uninsured-motorist (UM) coverage under S.C. Code Ann. § 38-77-150.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Leaving an injury crash is a misdemeanor unless great bodily injury or death results, in which case it is a felony (§ 56-5-1210(A)). For an unidentified driver, UM pays only if the crash was reported to police within a reasonable time and there was physical contact with the unknown vehicle, an independent witness who signs an affidavit, or an electronic recording of the crash (§ 38-77-170(A)).
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data — the felony error and the incomplete UM trigger are published twice over. Suggested: 'Yes. Leaving an injury crash is a crime under S.C. Code § 56-5-1210 (a felony when it causes great bodily injury or death). Your own uninsured-motorist coverage under § 38-77-150 covers an unidentified driver if you reported the crash promptly and there was physical contact, an independent witness, or a recording of the crash (§ 38-77-170).'

verifiedClaims.claim: your UM carrier steps in as if it were the at-fault driver's insurer — subject to your limits, which are often stackable across household vehicles.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Stackable for a Class I insured (named insured or resident relative) up to the coverage on the vehicle involved (§ 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire, 2013) — not generally 'across household vehicles'.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire Insurance, 406 S.C. 609 (2013)
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: '— subject to your limits, which a named insured or resident relative can sometimes stack from other household vehicles up to the coverage on the vehicle involved.'

verifiedClaims.claim: The driver's personal auto policy from their home state typically provides primary coverage and follows them into South Carolina; the rental company's policy may sit excess; and your own UM/UIM under S.C. Code Ann. §§ 38-77-150 and 38-77-160 fills the gap when those limits run out.
verifiedClaims.note: The UM/UIM leg is statutory. The primary/excess ordering between a renter's personal policy and the rental company's coverage is set by the policies and rental agreement, not by a South Carolina statute; 'typically' and 'may' keep it as characterization. Keep.

verifiedClaims.claim: Service on out-of-state defendants runs through the SC Director of Motor Vehicles under the non-resident motorist statute.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-9-350 (operation of a motor vehicle in South Carolina by a nonresident is 'equivalent to the appointment ... of the Director of the Department of Motor Vehicles ... to be his true and lawful attorney upon whom may be served all summons')
verifiedClaims.note: Verified. Optional: cite § 15-9-350.

verifiedClaims.claim: Probably yes, as long as you were 50% or less at fault. South Carolina follows modified comparative negligence with a 51% bar under Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243 (1991). If a jury finds you 20% at fault and the drunk driver 80%, your damages drop by 20%. At 51% or higher you recover nothing
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Rule, citation and arithmetic all correct.

verifiedClaims.claim: Sometimes. South Carolina has no separate dram-shop statute, but bars and restaurants can be held civilly liable under common-law negligence for knowingly serving alcohol to a visibly intoxicated patron who then injures someone.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Liability is negligence per se on the criminal sale statutes — § 61-4-580(A)(2) and § 61-6-2220 (knowing sale to an intoxicated person) — as recognized in Tobias v. Sports Club (1998) and Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill (2010, upholding a $10 million verdict); for claims arising after January 1, 2026, § 61-2-147 makes the licensee jointly and severally liable for 50% of actual damages when the verdict also runs against a driver charged with DUI.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 61-4-580, 61-6-2220, 61-2-147; Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill, 388 S.C. 407 (2010)
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. Suggested: 'Sometimes. South Carolina has no dram-shop act, but a bar or restaurant that knowingly serves a visibly intoxicated patron violates S.C. Code §§ 61-4-580 and 61-6-2220, and courts treat that as negligence per se (Tobias v. Sports Club; Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill). For crashes after January 1, 2026, § 61-2-147 can make the establishment jointly liable for half your damages when the driver is charged with DUI.' The evidence-preservation sentence that follows can stay.
